newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzania's flower growers urge more cargo flights.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania's flower growers urge more cargo flights.

text.p: Tanzania's rapidly growing horticulture industry has urged carriers to establish special cargo flights from these northern highlands to handle increasing exports of flowers to European markets.

Industry officials and growers said the areas under cultivation in the northern Arusha and Moshi region surrounding Mount Kilimanjaro and Mount Meru have increased from 40 hectares last yearto over 70 hectares this year from 40 hecatres last year.
And it is expected that figure will be further increased to over 100 hectares by the end of this year.

"It's getting more and more competitive here. Kenya is bigger than everyone of the flower exporting countries in Africa, but Tanzania could be much bigger than that if it wasn't for the problems of the airlines," said Adrian Moss, estate manager for Hortanzia Ltd.

"At the moment we have to sent all our flowers to Nairobi. We sent a full truck to Nairobi at least three times a week, because there is no cargo flights. There would be enough volume for at least two cargo flights a week," Moss told Reuters.
KLM Royal Dutch Airlines NV flies directly to the Kilimanjaro International Airport, located between the two northern cities of Arusha amd Moshi.

Hortanzia, backed by private Tanzanian and Kenyan investment, started business in 1993 with just two hectares and seven greenhouses, and already that business has been expanded to five hectares and 13 greenhouses.

Kenya, the biggest producer of cut flowers in Africa and number four in the world, exported flowers worth more than $100 million from some 1,200 hectares under cultivation in 1996, according to official figures.
Zimbabwe is the second biggest producer/exporter in Africa with some 650 hectares under cultivation.
About two-thirds of the production from Tanzania is exported to the Dutch flower auctions in Amsterdam while the remaining third is mostly exported to Frankfurt, according to the growers.

Heikki Niskala, farm manager for the biggest of the growers, the Dutch-backed Kiliflora Ltd, said the industry would continue to be expanded and it was likely that Tanzania within the next five to ten years would be the second biggest producer in Africa.
"It's been growing by 100 percent at least, by the hectare a year, over the last few years. It's definitively on the upswing, our neighbours are starting, there is lots of interest.

"By the end of the year there will be over a 100 hectares or even more. We ship in terms of weight 25 to 30 tonnes a week of flowers, in terms of stems we are looking at close to a million stems a week," Niskala said.
He said that with the still growing interest shown by new companies in addition to the six already operating, the flower exports should easily fill several freighters a week.

Kiliflora is only growing roses, mostly of the varieties known as First Red, Baroness and Escada, at the company's farm of 18 hectares, but cultivation on a new 12-hectare farm is expected to start by the beginning of next season in mid-August.
"Within three years from now the plan is to reach 50 hectares and by that time Kiliflora will become one of the biggest rose plantations in all of Africa.

"We want the airlines to come. At the moment we have about ten trucks a week going to Nairobi but there is a risk involved in trucking the flowers over the border to Nairobi. Any carrier which would set up a route out of Kilimanjaro would be welcomed," Niskala told Reuters.

Several carriers have studied the options for staring up a cargo line but to date the airlines have argued that there is not sufficient inbound cargo to make a freight flight economically viable, despite the large number of exports.

"Cargo capacity is small and the production is growing. The problem is that we don't have enough south-bound cargo, we have an average inbound cargo of three tonnes per flight," said Murtaza Versi, the local representative of KLM in Arusha.
"Here it will depends on the imports to Kilimanjaro. We should be getting a cargo growth area, but the size of growth will depend on the volume of inbound cargo," Versi told Reuters.

However, other airline sources close to the state-run Air Tanzania Corp said the national carrier now had started to realise the potential revenues it was loosing by the trucking of an estimated 400 cubic metres of flowers to Nairobi every week.
Both Air Tanzania and other private cargo companies were now discussing ways to set up alternative routes, the source said.

"Airfreight is a big issue here," said Niskala. "We have a better climate for flower growing here in Tanzania than in Zimbabwe so in five to ten years Tanzania could easily be number two or even three producer in Africa.

"The agricultural potential here is huge. There is potential for a carrier to come to kilimanjaro every day for flowers or vegetables and fruits. I hope that by the end of the year there will be a direct cargo link," Niskala said. --Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44-171-542-7706 Fax+5017
